title: Amazon: China-linked AI agents found and exploited MONAI Label zero-day in 11 minutes
subtitle: Threat intelligence researchers at Amazon say an unidentified Chinese-nexus actor ran the open-source Cairn agent framework to breach a university's medical imaging server and gain root access.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Amazon Threat Intelligence disclosed on Thursday that an unidentified Chinese-nexus actor used autonomous AI agents running the open-source Cairn framework to discover and exploit a zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source server used to annotate medical imaging research data. The flaw is a path traversal bug — an unauthenticated attacker can write files outside the storage folder — affecting MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default no-login configuration. Amazon found the operator's Cairn control panel exposed on the public internet without a password, which let researchers reconstruct the full intrusion. The agents moved from mapping the application's API to writing files in about 11 minutes, reached a university server in East Asia, and attained root. A second university network may have been compromised the same way but Amazon has not confirmed it.

The attribution is moderate confidence: Chinese-language prompts, Beijing-time-zone scripts, and targets of plausible strategic interest to Chinese collectors. The Register reports the Amazon disclosure follows earlier work by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that documented a Chinese operator running at least 105 Cairn-driven attacks. The MONAI Label developers have merged a fix into the source tree, but no patched release is available at the time of Amazon's post, per VentureBeat and The Hacker News. Administrators are advised to restrict network access to MONAI Label instances running 0.8.5 or earlier.

This is not the first fully autonomous agent-driven intrusion reported this year — Anthropic's September Threat Intelligence Report and Microsoft's October Digital Defense Report both described similar autonomous attack chains — but the 11-minute figure from a cold API map to a working exploit is a tighter data point than most prior disclosures. The defensive side of the ledger is not static either: OpenAI's Daybreak Red Team initiative and Microsoft's Project Perception shipped in the same window. What matters is the direction of the gap between offensive and defensive automation, and this quarter the offensive data points keep landing first.

A note for learners: defenders should treat 'exposed agent control panel' as the real story here. The agents did what agents do — enumerate APIs and probe weaknesses. What made the intrusion visible was an operational mistake: a C2 dashboard sitting on the open internet without a password. That mistake is how Amazon learned about the attack at all, and it is also how most agentic-threat research is going to get written in 2027. If you're running agent infrastructure, the first threat model to write is not about the models. It is about everything around them.
